title: A mind. A college. A world of ideas.
description: Trace Alan Turing’s educational connection to Cambridge, one sourced step at a time.
intro: Knowledge is made by people, and people are connected to places. This short route follows two relationships in the Wikidata record, from a mathematician to a college and its university.

transitions.heading: Begin with a place of study
transitions.text: Wikidata records King’s College as an institution where Alan Turing was educated. The relationship points from the person to the college: “educated at.”

transitions.heading: Look beyond the college
transitions.text: The next statement records King’s College as part of the University of Cambridge. A college and a university are distinct entities, joined here by a “part of” relationship.

summary: Two directed relationships turn a familiar name into a route through institutions. Continue from any topic to see what else the source records.

title: Follow an influence. Find an institution.
description: Ada Lovelace, Charles Babbage and a route through Cambridge’s colleges.
intro: An influence can be the beginning of a journey. This route follows a recorded connection between Ada Lovelace and Charles Babbage, then changes perspective from people to institutions.

transitions.heading: A recorded influence
transitions.text: The Wikidata record for Ada Lovelace includes an “influenced by” statement pointing to Charles Babbage. Influence is the claim made by this statement; it does not describe every aspect of their relationship.

transitions.heading: From a person to a college
transitions.text: Babbage’s record lists Trinity College under “educated at.” This identifies a place of study, without claiming that he completed a degree there.

transitions.heading: An institution within an institution
transitions.text: Trinity College is recorded as part of the University of Cambridge. The route now arrives at the university by following the college’s own statement.

summary: A route can cross different kinds of relationships without changing their direction or meaning. Try exploring Babbage to discover other recorded connections.

title: From a scientist to a city.
description: Follow Marie Curie’s connection to an institute and its recorded headquarters in Paris.
intro: Scientific work also has a geography. This route moves from Marie Curie to the Curie Institute, then to a city. The institute’s own account describes Curie’s role in creating its predecessor, the Institut du Radium.

transitions.heading: Follow an institutional connection
transitions.text: Wikidata lists the Curie Institute under Marie Curie’s “employer” relationships. Historical institutions can change their names and structure; the institute’s history provides context beyond this compact statement.

transitions.heading: Place the institute on the map
transitions.text: The institute’s record gives Paris as its headquarters location. This particular statement has no supporting reference recorded in the snapshot. The institute’s own site also lists Paris among its locations.

summary: A graph statement is a useful starting point, and its references and limitations matter. Follow the original sources when you want the fuller history.

title: From the Mona Lisa to Paris
description: Start with a painting and follow the records through its museum, country and capital.
intro: A painting, the museum that displays it, and the country and city around it are separate topics in Wikidata. Follow the relationship on each record to see how they fit together.

transitions.heading: Start in the gallery
transitions.text: Wikidata records the Louvre Museum as the painting’s location. The Louvre’s own collection record identifies it as the portrait of Lisa Gherardini and places it in the Salle des États.

transitions.heading: Follow the museum’s country
transitions.text: The museum’s country statement points to France. This step locates the institution at the country level.

transitions.heading: Return to the city
transitions.text: France’s capital statement points to Paris. The Louvre’s visitor information also gives its address in Paris, so the final topic brings the route back to the city where the painting is displayed.

summary: Location, country and capital describe three different relationships. Explore Paris or the Louvre to see what other collections and places the records connect.
